title: Removing the sampling caps
subtitle: From kernels that looked at fifty members and twelve hundred pairs to exact statistics over a hundred thousand members, by redesigning every kernel into one of three scaling classes

lede: The first generation of my cluster-metric kernels cheated, and I knew it. A cluster of a hundred thousand embeddings was scored from a sample of fifty members. The two-means split and the silhouette ran on fifty-member subsets. This is the story of taking every cap out. The early kernels were written one metric at a time, each with its own loop over members, each accumulating into global memory with atomics. At fifty members, contention on those atomics was invisible. At a hundred thousand it would have dominated, and a pairwise kernel over a hundred thousand members has five billion pairs. Sampling was the quick way to keep both problems out of sight.
quote: The numbers came back fast and they were estimates of the thing I wanted rather than the thing itself.
evidence: CUDA kernel development: every cluster-metric kernel sorted into three scaling classes, with Gram-bounded kernels refusing clusters above 2,000 members instead of sampling.
Embedding analytics and cluster metrics: pairwise statistics once capped at 1,225 pairs computed on every pair, for clusters of up to 100,000 members.
GPU performance engineering: a shared tile library with 6 accumulator types, and the centroid family at 46.67 ms for 100,000 members.
Regression testing for kernels: 20 legacy kernels kept, with sixteen tests against the CPU references, so each rewrite has a baseline.
author: Corey James
